My hon. friend outlined a kind of policy that he would put into effect when he came into power. He does not know what policy he would put into effect if he comes into power in two or three years, any more than I do. He will put into effect what his party behind him will support him in putting into effect, and that is where they are in a tremendous mix-up. Here is an hon. gentleman in my eye who is a protectionist down to his heels. Here is another gentleman who is either at present a member of the Farmers' party, or is being wooed with honeyed speeches and with languishing glances to become a member of the Liberal party, who believes that if they get into power they will simply treat the good old path of "free trade as they have it in England," and come ultimately to a free trade absolutism in this country of ours. How are they going to get together? Is there any Whip powerful enough to drive that side of the House into a union which will agree upon a tariff which will be laid upon any basis that my hon. friends can make a confession at the present time? It is all in the lap of the gods; it is all in the future, and we cannot see very well what it will be.
I do not know that I have anything more to say particularly. I take a little exception to the general principle my hon. friend laid down. He says that he would not be in favour of any policy which was founded upon protection, and he seems to think that a policy is not founded on protection when it proceeds on the assumption that you apply it to a certain industry which cannot live without it in this country, and apply it for a certain number of years until it gets able to live without it; he seems to think that in that case it is not a protectionist principle. My hon. friend made 'his confession full and free last year as to what he did down in beloved Nova Scotia, in the coal district, with regard to the iron industry. He saw there an industry which was not natural to this country, but which if subsidized for a sufficient length of time, might be built up, and in being built up would build up cities and towns and the surrounding countryside. He applied it, and it was successful; and it did build up an industry, and did build up the towns and the countryside. But that is not protection, according to iny hon. friend. I think that that is

protection. Nobody is such a dolt as to say: I am in favour of protection and I will apply it to everything, natural or unnatural, reasonable or unreasonable. The Prime Minister does not say that; we ourselves do not say that. That is purely a figment of the imagination of hon. gentlemen opposite. But we do say this: that in our country looked at from its own internal situation, and from its contiguity and its interchanges with the other nations of the world, some of the industries of this country do need protection, and so far as they do need protection to keep them on an even keel, we believe that the protective principle should be applied to them. My 'hon. friend would cut out every industry not .founded on the natural resources of this country. I go into other countries, many of them

I go into Great. Britain itself-and I find that some of its most flourishing industries, some of the greatest employment-givers that are to be found in Great Britain, are in the great cotton and the great woollen manufacturing districts of that country, and they do not raise an ounce of cotton in Great Britain, and not very much wool. Does my hon. friend take the position that when he comes into power he will rout out every industry in this country-the men to whom it pays wages, and the families it thereby supports-because its raw material is not raised in this country? I think it is a most excellent thing to do to get our raw materials from wherever you can get them economically, and bring them to our own country and manufacture them into the finished product, thereby employing our own men, giving support to their families, and building up our towns and cities and the country generally. That is good business. I would be sorry to see our woollen industries cut off. I would be sorry to see cut off our cotton industries, our sugar industries and all the other industries that depend for their raw materials upon other parts of the world. It is all a question of economical advantage applied in its widest sense, and we have to take into consideration when we are making up our minds with respect to this, more than simply the duty or tax.
I am a very moderate protectionist myself. I do not believe in protecting any industry beyond what is absolutely necessary to give it standing and competing power having regard to conditions in other countries of the world with which we compete.
My hon. friend presumes to speak for
the U. F. 0., for the Progressive party. The Progressive party will be heard from itself by-and-by, and it will say what it means. But that breach between your down-East protectionist Liberal, and the Farmers' organization in the far plains of the West, seems pretty difficult to heal. I have in my eye the wise countenance of my hon. friend from Cape Breton North and Victoria (Mr. McKenzie). I would like to see him and the leader of the Progressive party deploy and conduct their debate and lead up to a conclusion where the two could join as a happy family on a tariff policy for this country.
The hon. member will live to see it.

I have passed a considerable number of years in this world and, I do not say that I had hoped, but I rather had a premonition that my years were not so many in front of me as they are behind me, but if I am to fulfil the prophecy of my hon. friend from Cape Breton North and Victoria, I am quite sure that I shall live one hundred and fifty years longer.
My hon. friend from Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) was facetious over the tea industry; he amused the whole House, but it was such an extreme proposition upon which to found an argument, either for or against a policy, that I do not think it is necessary for me to follow that any further. Protection is not simply for the purpose of giving employment. Protection will run very wide indeed if its basic principle was that you must protect wherever you can get a band of men together, pay them wages, and keep them employed. Surely that is an extreme statement of protection. But protection, on the other hand, does have its interest in employment, and it does stand upon this basis, that the men of Canada have a right to employment in their own country so far as the economic conditions of the country make it possible, and so far as a policy of justice and of reasonableness can ensure that employment. There is a great difference between that and and the other. So far as I can see, my hon. friend would have no industries in this country which were not based upon native raw materials, native fuels, native water-power, and cheap labour, which he says now no longer exists. I should be very sorry to reduce to those limits any policy which I desired to follow.

One word more in conclusion, and that is by way of reply with reference to myself. My hon. friend said that when I got before the women's meeting in Montreal I had to be truthful. Well, that is a great compliment both to me and to the ladies. It shows that I have some quality which can be called upon, and it also shows that the ladies have an attribute that evokes the best that is in a man. Both these facts I endorse. However, what I said to the ladies in Montreal, if I may be allowed to advert to the matter, was this: That if there were in the United States of America demands that could not be supplied in that country itself, for any of the articles upon which they put a duty, my view was that those articles would probably be imported into the United States and that the United States consumer would pay the duty, or at least most of it; I thought that probably he would pay all; and that is where I thought I saw a little lifting in the cloud with reference to this emergency legislation. If, for instance, hard wheat is necessary in the United States of America for their milling operations and they have not sufficient of it in their own country and must, of necessity, have it to make their proper grades of flour, they will get it wherever they possibly can, no matter what they have to pay for it, and consequently the duty placed upon it by the United States Government in its tariff would not prevent much of that product from going into the United States. It would have a different effect according to the necessity for the product in the country which was importing it. That was the view I expressed, and I stand by it.
My hon. friend, I observe, also gave me a little dig in regard to my New York speech. He brought it up again to-day, and said he was sorry I went "whining to New York," asking them not to put a heavy tariff on Canadian products. Now, I did not whine before that audience in New York. Upon my word and honour, if my hon. friend will take my word for it, I did not whine in the least degree. In a conversation which I had, however,-a very confidential and intimate conversation with a certain audience in New York-
But published in the newspapers.

-I did bring to their notice this fact, that if a country wanted to retain the trade of another country it could not do so by having all the trade on one side, and that if it wanted us to buy, it ought to be somewhat careful and

should take thought before it barred us out from getting products into that country with which to pay for the goods we bought. That was my sentiment, and I may say to my hon. friend, to relieve his anxieties, that it was very well received indeed.

The hon. gentleman
made some converts. I read the speech.

Yes, and my
hon. friend, I am sure, believes every word I said.

Mr. ANDREW R. McMASTER (Brome) : It is always delightful to listen to the remarks of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster). I do not know whether there is a word in the English language that quite conveys the idea as to the nature of his speech in general, but I think there is a word in the Scottish tongue which aptly describes it: it is a delicious sort of daffing, and I must say that if the right hon. gentleman lives as long as he hopes to live in order to see the rapprochement-I, like himself, have sometimes to find a French word to express my meaning -between the hon. member for Cape Breton North and Victoria (Mr. McKenzie) and the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark) or the member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar) -if he reaches the mature span of 150 years, which we all trust he may, we may feel certain that his speeches will be syndicated and distributed among Life, Punch, Judge and Le Rire. I shall endeavour to pick out carefully and quietly the gems of thought which lie embedded in the setting of humour with which the hon. gentleman has surrounded his remarks.
Now, as regards the income tax, if I remember correctly, the members on this side of the House during the war pressed the Government of the day to introduce this form of taxation long before they took their courage in both hands and applied it; and therefore there is little or no credit to be taken by those gentlemen which does not in large measure belong to the members on this side of the House, or at least to the party which we represent. Let me make one suggestion in reference to the income tax, a suggestion which I submit for the consideration of the Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton). It is not quite fair that the rate of income tax should be as heavy upon earned incomes as it is upon revenue resulting from investments. A heavier rate should be imposed upon revenue from investments than is imposed

upon professional earnings or upon the salaries of men and women, because in one case you are taxing a person on the proceeds of his superfluity, while, in the other, you tax him upon his own efforts. Of course, my genial friend, the Minister of Trade and Commerce quite gave away the Government's case in regard to the difficulties, which the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) spoke about, in calculating the income tax, when he uttered the pious hope that his friend and colleague the Minister of Finance would arrange these matters better and avoid all this trouble in the future. May I point out to my right hon. friend that some of us have not the three-quarters of the highest possible assessment to send, as he generously did, to the Minister of Finance? And I would remind the right hon. gentleman, with all deference, that he is just as responsible to the House and to the country, as the Minister of Finance, for the form in which the income tax is now collected.
The minister (Sir George Foster) was recently at a meeting of the League of Nations, of which body great hopes have been entertained, and he returns to speak in terms of pride of the fact that we are spending only $2,500,000 on our navy,- little, if any, more than we did before the war. But, Mr. Speaker, the war was fought with the intention that we should set our heel upon militarism and enjoy better conditions in the future, and it is cold comfort indeed to say that we should be thankful because our naval expenditure has not risen. And I did not like the prophetic vein into which the minister then passed. He says, When the sky is brighter and economic conditions more favourable, then we will spend more money on the navy. I trust that will not come true. He then spoke of the burdens of the war. He said that he wished he could introduce the member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) to a knowledge of the burdens which he and his colleagues had borne during the war. Does the Minister of Trade and Commerce think for one moment that all the anxiety and all the burdens which the people of this country suffered during the war were suffered and borne by the members of the Administration? I venture to think, when I look down at the front row of this side of the House, that there were men who had anxieties and burdens, and troubles and sorrows, as grave as any that afflicted any member of the Government. The obligations did not cease when the war was over. Indeed they did not; and 201
could there have been, Mr. Speaker, any more generous affirmation of the willingness of the Liberals of this country to sup-* port their fair share of war expense than the words of the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's? I doubt if there could have been. I say this: that never did any government, in conducting a great war, find its hands so upheld by any Opposition as the Government of Canada found its hands upheld by the Liberal Opposition while the war was on. If there was any expenditure brought forward for the legitimate expenses of the war that the Liberals did not concur in, and if ever differences arose, it was because the Liberals felt from time to time that expenditures of an extravagant nature, or worse, were being incurred and we protested against them-we did our duty in that regard. When the minister tells us, Mr. Speaker, that demobilization is yet a matter for expense, I would say that is, in no small measure, due to the very extraordinarily large idea of what constitutes war expenditure, of what expense could properly be carried to demobilization, which the Government holds. For in the Public Accounts Committee, Mr. Speaker, the other day we found that the money paid to the lawyers in the Winnipeg strike for prosecuting men-among others one whose crime, was that he had quoted a verse out of the prophet Isaiah-that that expenditure, equivalent to $300 a day in some cases, was paid out of demobilization account. To that part of the "war expenditure" I object very strongly indeed; not perhaps to the Government having helped to have these men tried, but certainly to carrying the expenditure to an account in which it has no proper place. For it will not be forgotten that the war was over for more than a year, the fighting had ceased for more than a year or two years, before this expenditure was incurred. The minister says he is a very moderate protectionist. Well, one of my earliest recollections of political life is reading a speech of the Minister of Trade and Commerce in which he quoted:
That man's the true Conservative
Who lops the moulder'd branch away.
The minister shakes his head.
That was a speech made by Sir John Thompson,-just as good.
I accept the correction, but my hon. friend sat next to Sir John Thompson, he was, if I mistake not,

his Minister of Finance, and he took full responsibility, I am sure, for Sir John Thompson's statements. If I have credited the statement to the wrong man I beg my' hon. friend's pardon, but those were his sentiments at that time. But he goes on to say:-and I do not propose to deal very long with this part of his remarks-"I am a very moderate protectionist, I want to give an industry just enough to give it standing and competing power." Well, I would like to place this superstitious case before him,-I know that'with that nimbleness of mind which distinguishes him he will surely be able to follow my arguments. Let us suppose there are two factories

factory A and factory B. Factory A, is properly capitalized, a dollar was put in the treasury for every dollar of stock issued. Factory B was floated into existence in a company promotion, and every dollar of stock outstanding only represents fifty cents put in the treasury. Factory A is properly located, it went where railway communications were good, and where water communications were good. Factory B was seduced from a choice that it had made originally by a bonus, a vicious bonus, held out by some ambitious towns, and located in that town. Factory A is well run, and well managed; factory B is managed by the nephew of the principal shareholder who thinks much more of his golf score than he does of the success of the factory. Will the Minister of Trade and Commerce be able to tell me what rate of duty he would grant to both these industries in order to give them "standing and  competing power?" The Prime Minister of this country says "I am not a very high protectionist." It is wonderful, for protectionists, how they like to whittle down their protectionist beliefs-but that is just by the way.

Does the hon.
gentleman want an answer?

Of course, I always
like to hear you speak.

I shall be very glad to give my hon. friend an answer, he seems anxious for it. I would give them both the same protection, and I would base the protection on reasonable location, business management, and the like of that, and the man who did not manage his business efficiently should not call on the Government, surely, to give him a protection for his inefficiency.

That, of course,
would be the sensible thing to do.

Well, that is
what I would do.

But let me point out
that if factory B did not find a protection, say of twenty per cent, which was quite sufficient for factory A, sufficient to enable it to carry on, you would find the local member from the riding in which factory B is found, if he is a protectionist, importuning the country's administration for an increase of the duty, you would see him making a claim for "adequate protection" or "protection just enough to keep the wheels moving" as the Prime Minister once said.
Now let me, before I pass from this part of my subject, answer another argument advanced by the Minister of Trade and Commerce. He says that the duties, as a rule, are paid by the consumer. He is quite correct in that. He says that the Americans need our hard wheat; they will import our hard wheat and pay the duty. Yes, but the price of our hard wheat will rise and the advance in the price of our-
That is in the United States?

In the United States of course. Let me make my point perfectly clear. If this duty goes into effect in the United States, and a substantial rate is imposed on Canadian wheat, the American mills will yet require our hard wheat- they will yet have to import it. But that will increase the price to them and it will decrease the demand. It will tend to force the growing of wheat in the northern part of Dakota, and it will tend to hurt us, because you cannot apply a duty without raising the price to the consumer, and you cannot raise the price to the consumer without diminishing the demand. As things become inexpensive the demand for them increases; as things become expensive the demand for them diminishes; and you cannot get over economic laws, which after all exist whether the world is in turmoil or not.
I shall endeavour, Mr. Speaker, to extract from the mass of figures placed before the House yesterday by the Minister of Finance a few of the more salient items. The Minister of Trade and Commerce has claimed that this is a really economical Government-that appearances are deceptive and that the Government really possesses the virtue of economy. Well, the net debt on March 31, 1920, amounted to $2,248,868,623.79. During the year the net debt went up in round figures just $100,000,000. What did that mean? Taking our population at 8,500,000, the per

capita debt on March 31, 1920, amounted to $264.56, while on March 31 last it amounted to $276.48, a difference of $11.92. That is to say, every man, woman and child in the country owed in round figures $12 more this year than he or she did the year previous. That is a fact that I should like to have burned into the consciousness of the Canadian people. I should like to have every man and woman and every child of understanding years realize that this Government has increased the national debt by $12 per head during the past year. That meant that for every day during the fiscal year the debt had increased $277,720. During the short space of one day, while my hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce arose in the morning, pursued his avocations and retired to bed at night, the debt increased to that extent.
What are the other facts which I think should be brought home to the Canadian people? The total revenue for 1920 amounted to $349,746,334. The revenue for 1921 amounted to $82,500,000 morty But our expenditure amounted to $101,000,000 more than our revenue. So, although the revenue in 1921 rose by $82,500,000 over the year before, this spending aggregation was able to keep up with the increase of revenue-not only able to keep up with it, but to surpass it, so that at the end of the fiscal year we were $100,000,000 more deeply in debt than we were on March 31, 1920.
Shame!

The hon. member for Quebec East says "Shame." And it is a shame, because it was the duty of this Government tq cut down expenses, but they have not done so.
We have relied very much in this country, as is natural, upon our customs tariff as an engine for collecting revenue. It is interesting to note that the American Republic collected last year less than five per cent of ' their federal revenue through their customs tariff. Their total federal revenue amounted to $6,695,000,000, of which they collected $323,000,000 from their customs tariff, while we collected $163,000,000 from our customs tariff during the fiscal year ending March 31, 1921. In round figures, we, with 8,500,000 people, collected half as much money through our Customs as did the United States with their 110,000,000 of population.
The Minister of Finance has told us that the estimate of revenue to be collected under the existing laws amounts to
$372,600,000, but that it will require $591,437,000 to pay the estimated expenditure. That is to say, we will require to raise in order to meet our expenditure $228,800,000 more. He proposes to raise $62,760,000 of this by new taxes or by the increase of old taxes, and the balance of $156,000,000 will have to be borrowed. I cannot see how it can be done any other way. You can call it "refunding," taking the debt due by a railway and paying it off, borrowing the money for the purpose, but at any rate we have got to find the money either directly from taxation or indirectly by borrowing.
Let me pass for a moment, Mr. Speaker, to the trade question. Our total exports and imports the minister stated increased last year over the year before by almost $100,000,000. For ease of remembrance one can say that our total debt increased from one year to $100,000,000, that our expenditure increased about $100,000,000, and that our trade increased about $100,000,000. Then I would like to draw the attention of the minister-although he is not in his seat-to the fact that his comparison between the United States and Canada is totally misleading. I noticed some members on the other side of the House applauding when the Minister of Finance stated that the per capita trade of Canada was $293 and some odd cents while that of the United States was $127.78. There is no cause for any expression of exultation, for those figures really mean very little. The United States has varieties of climates and an industrial development which make it possibly the most self-contained country in the world, and as these figures relate merely to foreign trade they, of course, bear no relation to our figures.
The Minister of Finance seemed to express grave fears because our exchange with the United States was so unfavourable. May I state, Mr. Speaker, with all courtesy, that the fears of the hon. minister are based on the fallacy of the mercantile system and on the unsound theory of a favourable or unfavourable balance of trade? I have in this House on previous occasions by a short example shown the absurdity of that line of reasoning, but as a sound lesson cannot be too often inculcated I ask the indulgence of the House if I repeat what I have said before. If a vessel leaves Montreal, loaded, let us say, with a cargo of wheat worth $100,000-(I observe that the Minister of Trade and Commerce indi-

cates that I should designate the ship as one of our Canadian Merchant M-arine, but as, for the purposes of my illustration, the ship has to be lost, out of consideration for the Minister of Marine  I will not follow my hon. friend's sotto voce suggestion.) Well, this ship leaves Montreal loaded with $100,000 worth of wheat. It goes over to Liverpool and brings back a cargo of hardware worth, let us say $150,000. In that case exports are $100,000 and imports $150,000, and according to the protectionist mind that constitues an unfavourable balance of trade of $50,000 against Canada. But if on the way out the vessel is lost, then we have exports $100,000, imports nil; favourable balance of trade for Canada, $100,000. To reason on such a theory is to deceive and mislead oneself and to deceive and to mislead-unwittingly of course-others.
The Canadian nation does not buy from the United States. Individuals in Canada buy from individuals in the United States, and they only buy in that market if they get better value for their money. If they have to buy under a condition of depreciated currency, that, of course, is a pity, but as long as they get better value for their money than they would if they bought elsewhere they should be allowed to buy there, and for the Government to endeavour to interfere will merely hurt the country, not help it. In order to encourage the Minister of Finance I would.like to tell him also that the United States will not sell to us unless they get paid for what they sell; that they will not lend to us unless the security both for capital and for interest is satisfactory to them; and that a young country is bound to have an unfavourable balance of trade, especially if it has heavily indebted itself, as Canada has. A great deal of our exports, of course, go to pay the interest on our debt; the minister is perfectly right in what he says in that regard. But you will never help a country by interfering with the way private individuals propose to carry on their private business.
Now, the minister, after establishing the necessity for new taxes, comes down with his tax proposals, and his first tax proposal is a disguised but serious increase in duties. It was said of old-fashioned medical men that they were always willing to bleed their patients. If a man fell sick, they lanced him and bled him; if he had a relapse, they bled him again. The same principle seems to be upheld by my hon. friends opposite; they think that the only cure for the ills of the body politic

is more bleeding-in other words, more taxation.
First of all, then, I wish to.say that this taxation is disguised taxation; it is a disguised raising of the tariff schedules. The minister himself has not raised the schedules, but he has devised or some person has devised for him, this somewhat ingenious, but, I venture to assert, unwholesome, method of proceeding. A great many of the currencies of Europe are in a depreciated condition. The franc, usually worth twenty cents, is only worth nine; the lira, usually worth twenty cents, is worth less than six; the German mark, worth in normal times twenty-four cents, is worth less than two cents. What the minister proposes to do is this: in calculating the duty on an import an arbitrary depreciation of 50 per cent will be fixed, if the depreciation in fact is more than 50 per cent. The depreciation under 50 per cent will not enter into the calculation; no greater depreciation than 50 per cent will be recognized. Now, let me show you how that will work out. A man comes into the custom house .with an invoice of goods from France. Let us suppose that the franc, instead of being worth twenty cents, is worth ten. As that is no more than 50 per cent the francs will be turned into dollars on that basis and the duty assessed accordingly. But another man comes in with an invoice for Italian goods. Let us say that the lira, usually worth twenty cents, is only worth five. Now, that full depreciation will not be allowed; they will only allow it down to ten; the goods will be valued for duty purposes at twice their real value, and the duty imposed upon those goods will be twice as high as the schedule provides. The manufacturer, therefore, in Canada who is manufacturing goods which are made also in Italy is receiving twice as much protection as he got before. I think it is unsound; it will tend to keep goods out of the country, and it will have other effects which I will speak of in a moment. Then, suppose a man comes in with goods, let us say, from Austria or Germany. The mark has depreciated to less than two cents instead of its normal value of twenty-four cents. But these goods must be valued for duty purposes not at two cents but at twelve cents, to the mark six times as much, and the result will be that nothing will come in. The Minister of Finance is pursuing this mistaken and unsound fiscal policy with the idea that he is going to help Canada. I tell him that

he is going to hurt Canada, and I will show him exactly how it will work out.
How will it work with the United States?

It will work the other way with the United States. As a matter of fact, as United States money is at a premium, if you accept their invoices at their face value you would be reducing the duty. I understand that the minister proposes in the case of the United States, to bring about an assessment of duty on the real value of the article. I have no great objection to that. But I am dealing with the case of goods coming from a country in which the value of the currency has depreciated. First of all, Mr. Speaker, I tell the minister that so far as Canada is concerned he is hindering the economic recovery of Europe. As long as the middle kingdoms, Austria and Germany, are in the slough of economic despond there can be no real recovery in Europe. Now, does it affect continental Europe alone? No, it affects Great Britain also. Great Britain before the war exported to Germany as much merchandise as she exported to all her colonies. By helping to keep Europe in the slough of despond you tend to push the Mother Country down the same bank. You spoil our European market. You spoil our British market. If we are going to be kept out, to a certain extent at least, from the markets of the United States, we should wish to cultivate more strongly the British market. If you hurt the British market by hurting the European market, then you diminish the demand for the natural products of Canada. If you diminish the demand for the natural products of Canada, as the producers of natural products form a large part of the great consuming population of the country, you hurt the manufacturers themselves. This policy is a shortsighted, uneconomic one. It just tends to keep the world out of tune, to use the minister's own expression. It is a mistake, and in the long run, it can work only harm to the country.
At Six o'clock, the House took recess.
After Recess
The House resumed at Eight o'clock.

When
you, Mr. Speaker, so kindly, considered it six o'clock slightly before that hour, I had
been endeavouring to develop the point that the underhand method of raising the tariff adopted by the Minister of Finance, by giving an untrue and arbitrary value to the currency of a country depreciated in comparison with our own, would in the long run react upon ourselves to our disadvantage.
I now wish to develop the point and to show how the raising of these duties will affect the consumer in this country. For a long time, publicists in this country have been talking about reducing the high cost of living. At one time there was in Canada a Board of Commerce, of brief and un' happy memory, appointed for that very purpose. That Board of Commerce failed to reduce the high cost of living. It hardly came into being before it ceased to function, and now the Government is placing upon the statute book laws which will not only retard a reduction in the cost of living, but, on the contrary, will increase the cost of living. The safety of the world, the economic and, I think I might say, the social safety, of the world, in no small degree depends upon clearing the channels of trade, and this action on the part of the Government will tend not only to maintain the barriers which are now in the channels, but to insert other snags and quicksands in addition to those which are already there.
The next fiscal proposal of the Minister of Finance is the sales tax. The sales tax has been raised. It is now li per cent on a sale within Canada, 2i per cent on goods imported into Canada and where the sale is made directly from the manufacturer to the retailer, it is 3 per cent, if the transaction takes place in Canada, and 4 per cent if the transaction takes place between a vendor outside the country and a buyer within the country. I wish, first of all, to point out to the minister that this sales tax will take considerably more out of the pockets of the people than it will bring into the Treasury of the country. The manufacturer, in the first place, who sells to the wholesaler has to put on a tax of li per cent. That li per cent will forpi part of his cost of production. He will establish his profit on it. as well as on the primei cost of his goods, and will hand it on, plus the profit, to the wholesaler. The wholesaler, when he comes to sell to the retailer, will do the same thing, so that ultimately when the tax reaches the consumer, instead of being 3 or 4 per cent, it will amount to 4, 5 or 6 per cent. There is another objection to this tax, and it is this: One of the first maxims of taxation is that

the taxes should be determined by the ability of the taxpayer; they should be ability taxes, rather than consumption taxes. Now this is a consumption tax. If I am a man with a large family I shall have to pay more to the Government on account of this tax than a man who lives next door to me with an income just as large as mine, but who happens to be blessed with fewer children.
Oh, oh.

It is a blessing to have a larger number; the other man is blessed with fewer. No one can misunderstand what I said. The fact of the matter is that you are placing this tax most heavily on precisely those people who should not be called upon to bear it.
The next impropriety in the tax is this: You make the tax substantially heavier-3 per cent-when the sale is directly from the manufacturer to the retailer. Therefore, you encourage the middleman; you encourage that distributor whom it is desired to get rid of as far as possible. We want, if possible, in a civilized society to bring the producer and the consumer as closely as possible together. Every extra pair of hands through which goods pass increases the price without advantage either to the producer or to the consumer. Very often, of course, it is an advantage to have a middleman of this sort, but here there i is an artificial stimulation given to the existence of the middleman, and I humbly submit that that is unsound economics.
Again, the Minister of Finance has taxed the sales of imported goods more heavily than sales of goods manufactured in this country. What does that mean? It just means another indirect way of raising the tariff. We have a tariff, say, of 30 per cent, and remember, that the duties as a rule, as was admitted by the Minister of Trade and Commerce, are paid by the consumer. Now why should the consumer pay, let us say, 34 per cent-30 per cent tariff and the sales tax of 4 per cent-in respect of one article which is brought in from abroad, while he will only pay to the Government if he buys the article from a manufacturer within the country, 3 per cent? It is absolutely wrong. What should have been done was to make the sales tax as far as possible a counter-vailing excise tax. Then you would have got more money into the treasury, you would have placed no greater burden upon the consumer, and you would have protected your revenue, because what will happen under this sales tax is that the Government will

lose some revenue that it otherwise would have had. Customs duties are already high, and the sales tax placed on top of the customs duties may keep the goods out of the country, and thus the Government may get no revenue in respect of such goods whatsoever. In this connection, may I point out something which I noticed in the resolution? Flour is removed from the sales tax unless it is sold in packages of less than 48 pounds. If it is sold in packages of less than 48 pounds, it has to pay the sales tax. That is extremely unfair to the flour merchants and manufacturers who sell their wares in com-s paratively small parcels. It makes a distinction which I do not think is justified in equity. Why should the flour manufacturer who puts up flour in parcels under 48 pounds have to pay a tax while other manufacturers who do not sell in such small parcels are freed from the tax? It is unfair to the small flour miller, and more than that, it is unfair to the small family. I pointed out a moment ago how a tax was unfair to the large family. I suppose the Minister of Finance wanted to be fair in his unfairnesses, and now he has developed an unfairness to the small family. It is suggested to me by the hon. member for Chateauguay-Huntingdon (Mr. Robb), who is as conversant with the flour business as any one in the House, that the working man often buys his flour in small quantities, and if he buys' his flour from a miller who puts it up in small quantities, he will have to pay this tax, while if he is rich enough to buy a barrel at a time, or over 48 pounds, he will not have to pay the tax.
There is another matter to which I would invite the attention of the House. It is the increase of duties in connection with cocoa paste, cocoa beans, and cocoa-nuts. One would almost think that the Minister of Finance in his early days in visiting some exhibition had been very unfortunate at the cocoanut shy, because he has certainly come down heavily upon cocoanuts and all cocoa products. In our climate cocoa is a very valuable food, and anything that tends to raise its price is a mistake. It is a drink easily prepared, "grateful and comforting," as the advertisement of a certain brand states, and there is no reason why, when the minister is taxing whiskey, he should also turn his attention to cocoa. He has raised the tariff on cocoa paste or "liquor" from 3i cents and 4 cents per pound, the old rate, to 4 cents, 5 cents and 5 cents. Cocoa

paste or "liquor" sweetened is also raised, and preparations of cocoa or chocolate come now at a considerably higher rate than before. The old rate was 224 per cent, 274 per cent, 274 per cent; now it is 274 per cent, 35 per cent, and 35 per cent. I do protest against this taxing of one of the necessaries of life, because, besides being a healthful drink, it is a vital liquid food, and there is no social or economic reason why it should he raised in this fashion. Then arrowroot - has been singled out by the minister for attack. This is the invalid's food, and now the duty has been raised by 50 per cent. It used to be half a cent, a cent and a cent; now it is 4 cent, 14 cents, and 14 cents. I cannot see any good reason for this increase. Cocoa beans have been raised from free, 75, and 75, to free, $1.50 and $1.50.
I may be told that this is done in order that we may give a preference to the West Indies. I am anxious to trade with the West Indies and with any other country where I can get the best value for my money, hut I do protest against these efforts, which I do not think will be successful in the long run, to direct the stream of commerce at the expense of the Canadian consumer. The minister also feels that grape fruit should now be increased in price-for the increase in duty will no doubt bring about an increase in price- and even the small lime has not escaped his attention. He has pushed up the duty on these fruits by one half.
I do not propose to take up the time of the House any longer on this matter. In closing his remarks last evening, the Minister of Finance said1:
Mr. Speaker, we In Canada have a great task before us. The world is sadly out of tune. May we help in restoring harmony? Trust and confidence are sadly lacking. Class interests are advanced with selfish insistence. Unemployment, is with us. Faith in our fellow-men is weakened. Doubt of the future is often voiced.
I give the Minister of Finance credit for sincerity in the sentiments which I have just quoted, and I free him from any imputation of wrong intent in what he said. I believe he is as innocent of any wrong intention as he is powerless to control the spending proclivities of his colleagues as well as being quite unacquainted, it seems to me, with the fundamental laws of economics. He asks: "And what is the trouble?" I will endeavour, as briefly as I can, to tell him some things in which I think we are following wrong methods and in which I believe there is room for improvement. We are following an unsound
economic system. I know that our friends on the opposite side like to raise the bogey that we propose in one fell swoop to change the economic system followed for some time in this country and by so doing bring about distress, not because our cure is unwise, but because we want to apply it too quickly. We who believe in a low tariff, Mr. Speaker, are prepared to give every reasonable opportunity to manufacturers, or any other people who think that they are beneficiaries of the present system, to adjust themselves to new conditions; but we will not permit the foundation on which we propose to build our policy to be obscured. It is our firm conviction that protection has been a snare, a delusion and a mistake. That is my belief and the belief of a great number of people in Canada. Why have the people lost faith? I think that this Government has something to do with it. This Government has ceased to be representative; it has outlived the period of its usefulness, and should have gone to the country months if not years ago. It is holding on to office after the occasion for which it was given a mandate has expired, and I think that the best proof of this statement is the disinclination amounting to a practical refusal on the part of the Government to hold by-elections in time to allow the unrepresented portions of the country to be represented in this Parliament at the present time. The Government, I believe, is doing a wrong to the people in holding on to office in general, and it is doing a wrong to the people in refusing to hold byelections at such a time as will afford constituencies unrepresented an opportunity to elect members to represent them in this House. There has also been another practice on the part of the Government which has tended to undermine public confidence in public men, and that is the attempt that has been made by members of the Cabinet and other gentlemen on the other side to seduce men from their political allegiance.
Oh, oh.

Those hon. gentlemen who laugh and say "Oh, oh," know as well as I do that what I say is absolutely true. Recently there has occurred in this House an incident which is also calculated to undermine the confidence which the public should have in public men. I propose to refer to this incident for two reasons. In the first place, I may say that I was engaged in a by-election at which the minister in question was elected. He asked the people of St. John city and county to elect

him for certain reasons. He said: "I will go to Ottawa, not as a Liberal or a Conservative, but to represent, first, the port of St. John, secondly the people of St. John, thirdly, the province of New Brunswick, and then the Dominion of Canada." On that occasion I protested against that method of political appeal and I warned the people of St. John that that was not a proper sentiment to be uttered by a public man. My words were not heeded, but I have in my hand to-night the proof that what I said was wise and true; and it would have been well if my audience had harkened to me. Again, in this House, earlier in the session, I introduced a Bill for the purpose of dissociating public men from their private interests. I proposed that men who entered the Cabinet should cease to act as directors of incorporated companies. The Government spoke and voted against that Bill. Some were kind enough to say that they approved of the ideas which I entertained but that I was entering on the field of private honour, and that private honour was best left to private honour and legislation would be unwise. Under these circumstances I beg leave of the House to bring this matter before it: On January 13, 1921, on the paper of the Department of Customs and Inland Revenue, the following letter was 'written:
French Purchasing Commission,
Care of French Embassy,
London, E.C., England.
Dear Sirs,-I am informed that your Government will have quite a few French steamers taking grain from the port of Saint John, N.B., Canada this winter. .
The firm of Nagle and Wigmore of which I am a member are very anxious to secure this business. We are the largest firm of shipbrokers in Saint John and have done a very large amount of business along these lines.
We have our own tow-boats, tend to all stevedoring and all matters in connection with the general brokerage business.
As you are no doubt aware. I am Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue in the Canadian Government and I spoke to Sir George Foster, my colleague in the Cabinet who has just returned from England being Canada's representative at the League of Nations' conference which has just been concluded at Geneva and he advised me to write to you.
We are in a position to handle your business to your satisfaction and would refer you to the Bank of Nova Scotia as to our financial ability.
We are agents for the Canada Steamships Lines Limited, the Compagnie Canadienne Transatlantique, Limited, the Fracanda Line and the Acadian Shipping Company, Limited.
I would very much appreciate your giving us your business.
Thanking you in anticipation,
I remain,
Tours very truly,
R. W. Wigmore.
Now I do not propose to animadvert at any length on the discredit of this communication or to reproach the minister for, having written it. I merely state that it shows the minister is not familiar with the conventionalities, or the proprieties, or. even the decencies of public life; but what I do want to bring before the House and the country is the attitude which the Prime Minister has assumed in connection with this matter. The Prime Minister is the master, when he desires it, of clear expression, and I have read with care in Hansard what he said when this matter was brought to his attention in the House. His clarity on that occasion was conspicuous by its absence. He surrounded his thought in a cloud of words, but no word of disapproval of this action escaped his lips:	'
It is not for me to approve or disapprove-
He said:
-of conduct particularly, unless such conduct is of a character inconsistent with the duties of the minister as a minister. ... I must say that I was not able in this case to discern conduct of any corrupt or culpable nature.
If the Prime Minister of Canada is not able to discover anything of a culpable nature in regard to a letter of this sort, then it is the duty of the Opposition to point it out to him as clearly and as emphatically as possible. I say that such action on the part of a minister of the Crown is first of all unfair, and grossly unfair, to the electors who elected him. The electors of St. John may have come to the conclusion that it is quite proper to elect a man to represent their port first, their city next, their province third, and then the Dominion of Canada; but they never would come to the conclusion that his first duty was to represent the stevedoring firm of Nagle and Wigmore. It is grossly unfair to the electors of St. John who elected him. Then I say it is lacking in dignity. I could no more imagine certain members of this Government doing such a thing than I could imagine them flying, but if they remain silent, if they do not protest, then, to a certain degree at least, they must bear a share of the responsibility.
The next point I want to make, Mr. Speaker, is that it is dangerous to the state. Some years ago there was a trade arrangement negotiated in Washington. One of the ministers of the Crown who went to Washington to negotiate that trade arrangement was then Minister of Customs the late deeply regretted Hon.

William Paterson, and it is quite possible if this Government should maintain itself in office for some time longer that the Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue may be sent to Paris to negotiate a trade agreement with France. If he was there, and if the discussion waxed somewhat warm as to whether this concession or that concession should be granted to Canada, would not the minister be in a nice position if one of the officials in the French Foreign Office, who perhaps had been attached to this Purchasing Commission in London, said:	"Well, Monsieur Wigmore
you should be a little easy with us. Do not forget we gave an extremely lucrative contract a couple of years ago to your firm of Nagle and Wigmore?" For a minister of the Crown to solicit business for his firm from a foreign government, or any department of a foreign government, or any commission of a foreign government, is unwise, in fact dangerous, to the state. It may be summed up as a prostitution of public position to promote private profit.
What may it lead to? If it is correcr, if it is proper, for the minister to solicit business from a foreign government, why should it not be proper for him to solicit business from another department, or a commission,'in his own country? There may be a difference-no doubt the Prime Minister, the Minister of Justice or the member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) can draw the distinction-but what is the gravaman of the charge? The gravaman of the charge is that a man uses his public office to further his private business and the impropriety would be merely a question of degree. I am sorry the Prime Minister is not in his place for it is with him I wish to deal. It is with his failure to disapprove of this conduct with which I wish to deal. If the Prime Minister says that it is all right, what objection could there be to one minister asking another to promote the interests of the companies in which that first minister is engaged? I have on my desk before me a little book called "Landor's Imaginary Conversations." There you find a conversation between Henry VIII and Anne Boleyn. You find one between Queen Mary and Bothwell, and between Cromwell and Walter Noble. I have, along these lines, prepared two letters. They are absolutely imaginary; there is no intention in my mind to assert for a moment that it is possible for the man, who is supposed to have written this imaginary letter to have really written it-I want that distinctly understood. But I say once you throw the door open this is what we may find in the case of a man, perhaps of not as high character as those who are at present in the cabinet. This is the imaginary letter:

I again say that it is an imaginary letter, and I do not imply that the gentleman whose name I will read out as the fictitious author would have written such a letter. I merely place this before the House and before the country to show how far the matter may go if the Prime Minister's view is taken that such conduct as that of the Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue shall pass without any expression of disapproval.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to a point of order. I do not know whether I am correct or not
You are not.

I am always glad, Mr. Speaker, to accept your ruling on matters of parliamentary etiquette. I am not prepared to accept your ruling on questions of good taste; I believe that I am sufficiently endowed to deal with such questions myse'"

speechtext: The hon. member, if he questions the ruling of the Chair, knows his proper remedy under the circumstances. I wish to say, Mr. Speaker, that I take no objection to your ruling. I take objection to a gratuitous remark as to whether I am proceeding in good taste or not, because I do not believe that is within your province.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I believe it is within the province of the Chair, subject always to its occupant having the confidence of the House, to see that the proceedings of Parliament are conducted in a proper spirit and with due decorfim. I think the hon. member will find that that is true in all British deliberative assemblies. But I do not think the hon. member should take the attitude that he has taken in respect to a remark made by the Chair, because there was no intention whatsoever to unduly reflect upon him. It is, however, quite proper for the Chair, to direct the attention of the House to the circumstance that it was questionable whether the hon. member was proceeding in good taste or not.
