Further than that I cannot go.

I have endeavoured
to show what the failure to disapprove of this sort of action may lead to. I have done it in such a way as to amply prove my case, because the Minister of Marine and Fisheries resents so strongly the idea of being connected with such a letter that he protests in the most emphatic terms against his name being attached to it even

when it is declared in the most unequivocal terms to be purely an imaginary letter. We have to see in this House that public confidence is restored. It is not for the Prime Minister to excuse the inexcusable, to justify the unjustifiable, and to defend the wrong. It would have been more fitting,
I submit, for the Prime Minister not to have endeavoured to palliate the conduct of his colleague but to have kindly reproved him. It is along the line of restoring confidence that we must proceed, and we can only restore confidence when the men and women of this country know that the members of this House are seeking no selfish or private interests but only the welfare of the state.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) said this afternoon that there was no free trade issue in this country; that the Liberal party had never advocated free trade; and he assumed to speak for the Progressive party, saying that that party had never committed itself to free trade. In view of this statement by the hon. gentleman I would like to quote to the House a plank of the Liberal platform of 1893, which says:
We denounce the principle of protection as radically unsound and unjust to the masses of the people, and we declare our conviction that any tariff changes based on that principle must fail to afford relief to the trouble under which this country labours.
That was the platform of the Liberal party in 1893, and the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's was then a prominent member of the Liberal party and had a part, I would assume, in framing that particular part of it. But in speaking on the Budget last year the hon. member said:
I think we will find that we are all prone, in framing platforms, to put things perhaps a little more strongly than is wise, and we all find that we have, when we come to the responsibility of office, to modify our views.
With a wave of his hand the hon. member sweeps away the [pledge that Was given by the party to which he belonged in 1893 and which was backed up by the right hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier in these words:
If the liberals are successful they will cut off the head of protection absolutely and trample on its body. We will tax for revenue but not one cent for protection.
What does that pledge mean? Has. it any meaning whatever? Does it convey
any thought to the people of the country? What do these words of Sir Richard Cartwright mean:
Our policy is death to protection. Our policy from first to last has been to destroy this villainous system of protection which has been grinding out the vitals of the country.
Do these words mean nothing? Were they intended to * impress the public mind or not? Sir Louis Davies said:
We are attacking this policy year after year. This is an accursed system-a system accursed of God and man.
Well, it has been cursed enough by certain men on the other side, there is no doubt about that. But the hon". member for Shelburne and Queen's, with a wave of his hand, says: The best evidence we can give the people that the Liberal party is not a free trade party, never was a free trade party, never had any thought of adopting free trade, is that notwithstanding our very definite and specific pledges along that line, made to the people of Canada and repeated from one end of the country to the other, for fifteen years we have made no attempt whatever to carry out our pledges. And he wants the people of the country, Mr. Speaker, to accept that explanation. In fact, he told us this afternoon that just as the people accepted their statements in 1896 they would accept their statments in the election whenever it should come, be it this year or next. But there is this difference, Sir: In 1896 the people had had no experience in the deliberate breaking of solemn pledges made by the leaders of a party, but in the fifteen years that these hon. gentlemen were in power they demonstrated how little dependence could be placed by the people in any promise which they made. I say, therefore, that when the hon. gentleman and his friends again face the electors of Canada they will not find the people quite as credulous, quite as ready to believe their statements and accept their pledges, as they found them in 1896.
The hon. member for Brome (Mr. Mc-Master) has at times advocated free trade in this House with a reverence which would almost make one believe that the free trade doctrine was a part of the Sermon on the Mount, but in practice the hon. gentleman has paid just as little attention to that doctrine as a heathen would pay to the doctrine of Christianity. That is the difference between the free trade theorist when he advocates his theory and the free trader when he comes down to practical politics. The hon. gentleman has frequently posed in this House as a free trade economic expert,

and on many occasions he has given us some excellent illustrations of the arbitrary use of a specialized imagination. Today, however, he has gone beyond that and has attempted to place this specialized imagination of his in book form so that it may be handed down to posterity. The hon. member made an attack upon hon. members on this side and in order to drive home his attack he professed to read what he called imaginary letters. He questioned the propriety of a minister of the Crown having anything to do with a business enterprise, advertising himself because he was a minister of the Crown as connected with a business enterprise. The hon. gentleman, I think, has forgotten some things which have taken place in this country within recent years. I would like to draw his attention to an advertisement which appears in the Canadian Law List of 1910. It is an advertisement which takes up the whole of one page; there is nothing imaginary about it; it is here in black and white. It is the advertisement of a firm described as "Murphy and Fisher, Barristers, Solicitors, Parliamentary, Departmental and Patent Office Agents; Practice Before Railway Commission," and the members of the firm are Harold Fisher and the Hon. Charles Murphy, who was at that time a member of the Liberal Government. What, may I ask, was the purpose of putting this advertisement in this book if it was not to secure business for that firm? Why should they call particular attention to the fact that they were parliamentary, departmental and patent office agents if it was not to try to get the public to deal with them, and why should they call attention to the fact that one of the members of the firm had the prestige of a position in the government of the day? Did that call forth any adverse criticism from the member from Brome? As a lawyer he would naturally look over this list and know that this advertisement was there; did it bring anything from him? Not that we have ever heard of. Then, again, I call attention to the Canadian Law List of 1911, and in that I find another firm advertising their wares-Gouin, Lemieux, Murphy and Berard, and it goes on to tell us who they were: "Sir Lomer Gouin, Premier of Quebec; Hon. R. Lemieux, C.R., M.P., Postmaster General." What was the idea of putting "Postmaster General" in there if it was not especially to call the attention of the public to their peculiar fitness or ability to deal with matters as a firm?
I might refer the House to the Canadian Almanac of 1911, which contains, amongst 
other advertisements, an advertisement containing the name of the hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Bureau), and the information that he was at that time Solicitor General.
What year is that?

The Canadian Almanac of 1911. It occurs to me that the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) is living in a glass house when he is attempting to throw these stones; that in this connection, as in connection with everything-with which he has had anything to do with our public life, trade matters and the like, my hon friend has always had two different kinds of songs. One song he sings, for instance, when he wants to pose as a great free trader, and another song he sings, as he did before the Liberal Convention in 1919 in this city, when he wants to get a little bit of support from those manufacturers whom he is sometimes disposed to speak of very harshly on the floor of this House. We have various kinds of free traders. We have in this House a number of free traders who seem to agree as regards what they oppose, but who never seem to be able to agree on any definite, constructive policy. One finds in the free-trade doctrine something that he cannot just swallow or agree with; another finds something else, and when the question is one of playing politics, even the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark), who has posed repeatedly in this House and in this country as an out-and-out, uncompromising, free trader, finds himself playing the game of practical politics. I will quote the hon. member's words in that regard a little later on. The hon. membe. for Brome (Mr. McMaster) a couple of years ago found himself in a very much different position from that in which he finds himself to-day. On that occasion he moved an amendment, and he was not quite as much in agreement with the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) as he appears to be now. On that occasion the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's did not occupy a sea: on that side of the House. The hon. member for Brome, I remember, pictured the ship of state with Sir Thomas White as captain, and he pictured the captain of the ship as being threatened by what he called the starboard watch and the port watch. Then he added these words:
Then approaches with swift tread the quartermaster from Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding), and he says: "Captain, I belong neither to the starboard watch nor to the port watch. I

believe in party government, a party of one. I tender you, captain, my independent support until I consider it is time for me and my friends to unite and make you walk the plank." I do not know whether I can congratulate or commiserate the Acting Prime Minister, the captain of the ship, for the support he gets from the eloquent and the revered quartermaster from Shelburne and Queen's.
The hon. member for Brome has become quite docile since then. He has handed over the particular portfolio that formerly belonged to him as the great resoluter of the House. He sits mildly and quietly several seats back behind the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's, who now moves the resolutions and passes the word back to the hon. member for Brome to play the soft pedal on his free-trade business for a while "until we see if we cannot fool the people as we did in 1896."
The hon. member for Brome, in his speech, rather blamed Canada for preventing Europe from getting back to normal * conditions. I do not know that those were his exact words, but I think they convey his idea fairly well. He rather
9 p.m. objected to the fact that we did not allow German goods, for instance, to come into Canada and assess them at the present exchange value of the German mark. I have heard what seem to me to be same very curious arguments from my hon. friend, but I do not think I have ever heard anything which has struck me as being quite as peculiar as that argument. If we were to follow his lead- and he says that the German mark is worth only about two cents-that would mean that German goods made by the cheap labour of Germany-German labour that is hardly worth anything-would be allowed to come into this country and be assessed at an ad valorem valuation according to the present value of the German mark. He might as well have no tax on the goods at all. He is taking a roundabout way of advocating what is practically free trade. There are in this country enough men walking the streets looking for work; we have made sacrifices enough as a country in the war that we went through, and I for one would strongly object to allowing German and Austrian made goods to come into this country to take the place of goods manufactured by our Canadians, while our Canadians walk the streets of our cities looking for work. That is the position taken by the hon. member for Brome, and I take issue with him on that point just as strongly as it is possible to do so.	'
I want to say a few words in regard to the tariff, and I desire to preface my remarks by this statement. We have reached a time-in fact, in my judgment, we have long since passed the time in this country -when we should have a permanent tariff commission to gather facts for the information of whatever Government is in power and for the members of Parliament, a tariff commission similar to the one which is in existence on the other side of the line and which, according to expressions of opinion of their statesmen, has done magnificent work for that country. The appointment of such a tariff commission would go a long way towards resoring public confidence in this or any subsequent Parliament in its dealing with tariff matters. Satisfy the public that you have the facts before you; that this House is in a position to deal with known facts, and I am convinced that you will find very few people in Canada who are free traders. I believe that the vast majority of the people' of this country are in favour of moderate protection and that they will support a government which has that for its policy, if they are convinced that the government is dealing in a scientific way with the tariff on absolutely irrefutable facts for a basis.
In connection with what has taken place in this country during the past few years, may I say that as regards the public debt in Canada, our debt in March, 1911, was $340,000,000, and in 1914 on March, 31, $333,300,000. That is to say, between 1911 and 1914 there was a reduction of the debt of $6,700,000. Then the war came on. I want to say this, and only this in regard to our debt. It is, of course, very large but I do not think one needs spend time in attempting to prove that the increase in our debt is due entirely to the war and to the needs growing out of the war. I obtained from the Finance Department last year some figures in regard to this, and I propose to place them on Hansard. The interest on the war portion of our debt, on soldiers' civil re-establishment, and pensions, up to March 31, 1920, amounted to $1,996,000,000. I think I am right in quoting from the speech of the Minister of Finance yesterday that the amount spent along these lines in the last fiscal year was $225,000,000. That would make a total up to the end of the last fiscal year of $2,221,000,000; that is the amount of money spent in connection with the war-war interest, soldiers' pensions, soldiers' civil re-establishment, and

so on. Now when we take that into consideration, I think that this country has made a splendid showing so far as its finances are concerned. I believe that in the period from 1911 to 1914, notwithstanding the fact that the people of Canada had contributed in Victory Loans about $1,000,000,000, and large amounts also in voluntary contributions, the deposits of the people in our savings banks increased by 87 per cent, which was 7 per cent more than the increase of deposits of the people of the United States for exactly the same period. Having regard to these figures, and the fact that the Government has during the years of the war not only kept up the grants to agriculture, but multiplied those grants by four, and given special grants in many other directions to assist the people generally. I think that the financial position of this country is one of which we need not be ashamed.
Now in regard to Budgets. The first ' Budget after the 1911 election was delivered in March 1912. There were no tariff changes in that Budget. In 1913 the next Budget was delivered. It reduced the duty on cement from 12i to 10 cents per hundredweight, and from 431 to 35 cents per barrel of 350 pounds; typesetting and type-casting machines bearing a duty of 20 per cent were made free; traction ditching machines, bearing a duty of 27i per cent, were made free; sugar duties in the general tariff were reduced from $1.24i to $1,071 per cwt. So, as far as that Budget is concerned, I do not think that anybody can claim that its tendency was in the direction of greater protection, but rather in the. direction of lowering the duties.
In April 1914 the next Budget was brought down. A duty was imposed in that Budget on wire rods, but an exception was made where those wire rods entered into the manufacture of fencing. The duty on bituminous coal was removed when such coal was used for making coke. The duty on binders, mowers and reapers was reduced from 171 to 121 per cent. In that Budget of 1914 I think that any person who is disposed to be fair will say that the tendency was in the direction of lowering, rather than increasing the duties.
We come to 1915. The war was on then, and the necessity for raising revenue was pressing very strongly upon the Government. The War Revenue tax of 71 per cent and 5 per cent was added. There was a general addition of these duties, but certain exceptions were made, and I wish to call attention to those exceptions because

they indicate a desire on the part of the Government to give the farmer the benefit of as low a duty as possible. The exception to the addition of the 5 and 71 per cent duties were wheat, wheat flour, tea, sugar, anthracite coal, binder twine, binders, mowers, reapers, ditching machines, and salt for fishermen. Special taxes were imposed on banks, trust companies, -loan companies, and express companies. Then there was a tax on cheques and railway tickets, and an increase in the letter postage. I would again call attention to the fact that in that Budget preference was given to the farmer.
The next Budget was brought down in February 1916. It raised the duty on apples to 90 cents a barrel; the duty on petroleum oils was increased half a cent a gallon, and The Business Profits tax was imposed.
In 1917 there were no tariff changes, but some changes were made in the Business Profits tax and the Income tax.
We come now to the Budget of 1918, when the senior member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean) was Acting Minister of Finance. There were no tariff changes to speak of in that Budget. A duty was imposed on tea and some change was made in the duties on coffee and chickory. The excise duties were increased on cigars. I wish to quote briefly from the speech of the hon. member for Halifax, then Acting Minister of Finance (Hansard, 1918, P. 1256) :
To redress the adverse rate of exchange with the United States, we must lessen our imports from that country, or the United States must buy more from us.
I quote those words because they are very much in line with the words that were used a year later in this House by the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar).
Now I want particularly to call attention to what took pace in the Budget of 1919. The Customs War Revenue Tax which had been imposed in 1915 of 5 and 7i per cent was removed entirely with regard to the British and practically repealed in regard to the general tariff. Both the 5 per cent and the 7i per cent, which had been imposed in 1915 and which I think was unanimously accepted by the House,-although I am not sure of that statement,-were repealed on food stuffs, linen, cotton and woollen clothing, boots and shoes, fur caps and fur clothing, hats, caps, bonnets, gloves, mitts, collars and cuffs, hides, skins, leather, harness and saddlery, agricultural implements, petroleum, oils, mining machinery and bituminous coal. In addition to the removal of the 5 per cent and the 7h per cent, fur-

ther reductions were made in the tariff rates as they had existed since 1907. There was a reduction on coffee of 5 cents, and on tea of 3 cents per pound; wheat, wheat flour and potatoes were included in the free list, potatoes being an addition thereto. The general tariff on agricultural implements was reduced from 27h per cent, first, by taking off the 71 per cent which had been added in 1915, and then by taking off an additional 5 per cent. That is to say, the duty was brought down to 15 per cent on cultivators, harrows, horse rakes, seed drills, manure spreaders and weeders; and there was a reduction from 271 per cent to 171 per cent on ploughs, windmills, portable engines, and traction engines for farm purposes, horse powers, threshing machines, and separators. There was a reduction from 321 per cent to 20 per cent on hay loaders, potato diggers, feed cutters, grain crushers, fanning mills, hay tedders, field rollers, farm wagons, post hole diggers, and other agricultural implements. The duty on cement was reduced from 10'to 8 cents per hundred pounds. The above changes which, as hon. members can all see mostly affected the farmers, meant a tariff reduction and a consequent loss of revenue of over $17,000,000.
Now, Sir, I have called particular attention to this because certain hon. gentlemen in this House, who sit^ over to my right and call themselves the Progressive party, showed an attitude in regard to that Budget which has always seemed to me most peculiar and inconsistent. On that occasion the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) moved an amendment to that Budget, which called for free foodstuffs and free machinery, and the adoption of the Reciprocity Pact of 1911. There was a manifest con-tradition in the terms of the amendment, inasmuch as if you adopted the Reciprocity Pact of 1911 you would raise the duties on agricultural implements higher than they were at that particular time. At the same time, however, the amendment called for free machinery. On that occasion the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar), the leader of the Progressive party, said, as recorded at page 3331 of Hansard: "This is a protectionist Budget." That was his opinion at that time. I agree that it was a moderately protective Budget. But what did the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark) say in regard to the Budget on that occasion? I quote his words from page 3381 of Hansard. Referring to the statement of the hon. member for Marquette, he said:
"I cannot quite agree with my hon. friend from Marquette... I think a fairer thing would be to define it-and I think history will so define it-as a Budget tending towards free trade. I am particularly grateful for the Budget."
How did he show his gratitude? He showed it by voting against that Budget, for which he said he was particularly grateful. Again, as will be seen on the same page, he said:
The Budget has this advantage at least over the amendment: that it can be pointed to by its authors as having done something. . . we must give a great deal of credit to peopie who do things in preference to those who. . . . only profess them.
And then he manifested the sincerity of his desire to give credit to people who do things, rather than to those who only profess to do them, by voting for the amendment. He voted in support of those who only made a profession and against those who were really doing something. Again, he said, in referring to the Budget of 1919:
The reciprocity agreement is very largely embodied in the Budget proposals.
Well, the reciprocity agreement, I have always been led to suppose, was something which my hon. friend from Red Deer and those who sit around him, were particularly favourably disposed towards. Yet, notwithstanding his assertion that the reciprocity ' agreement was largely embodied in the Budget proposals, he registered his vote against the Budget. And again, he says:
The Government has also imposed fairly steep direct taxation-
Another thing which was in keeping with what the hon. gentleman and his party were advocating. ,
Here the Budget has a very great advantage over the amendment.
But for the purposes of practical politics, the hon. member for Red Deer could not and did not support the Budget, although in many respects, he pointed out its superiority to the amendment proposed. Again in the Budget debate in May, 1920, to which an amendment was moved by the member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding), I find these words of the hon. member for Red Deer. On page 2671, he is reported as saying:
I should have hoped that the amendment would have contained more milk and less water under those circumstances, and would have been less a Shilly-shally, temporizing and opportunist piece of print.
Now, that is hitting pretty hard in one sentence; I do not know what more the hon. member could have crowded into a

single sentence'in the way of condemnation of the amendment. He describes it as nothing but milk and water, and a shillyshally temporising opportunist piece of print. That was the language which he used to characterize the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's on that occasion. Nevertheless, he proceeded to record his vote in favour of the said shilly-shally temporising milk and water amendment.
I should like to call the attention of hon. members and the attention of the people of the country, especially the farmers, to the fact that when the Government made the proposition in June, 1919, to lower the duties on farm implements, making very substantial reductions all along the line, the hon. gentleman from Red Deer, as well as the member for Marquette, and those who sit around him, and who have frequently stated in this House and to the country that all duties should1 be removed from farm implements, recorded their votes against that budget which was making more sweeping reductions on farm implements than had ever been made in the history of this country, from Confederation down to the present time, by any former Government. Their attitude was one of hostility and absolute inconsistency. Party politics is what they were playing just as they were playing party politics this session in asking this House to accept the reciprocity pact which, if accepted would raise the duty on farm implements, and which, in another breath and in their platform, they say should be free. Sir, I want to call your attention to this: The tariff under the Laurier Government on dutiable goods averaged 281 per cent: the tariff now on dutiable goods averages 23 per cent. The tariff prior to 1911 on all imports, dutiable and free, amounted to 16.5 per cent; the tariff now on all imports, dutiable and free, averages less than 15 per cent. The tariff on farm implements prior to 1911 averaged 20.18 per cent; the tariff on farm implements under the reciprocity pact averaged 17.33 per cent; and the tariff on farm implements to-day, averages 14.64 per cent.
But, Sir, while I call your attention to the fact that the tariff on farm implements is lower to-day than ever before in the history of this country, may I also call your attention to the fact that the leader of the Progressive party, the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar), is also president of the Grain Growers' Grain Company.

While objecting to this duty of 12i per cent on binders, mowers, and reapers as being extortionate and as robbing the farmers, the company of which he is president, according to the sworn evidence of Mr. Rice Jones, their $13,000 manager, which evidence I have under my hand, collected in profits out of the pockets of the farmers 21.06 per cent on farm implements. Oh, consistency thou art a jewel! Here we have the president of the Grain Growers' Grain Company, the hon. member for Marquette, the leader of the Progressive party-and who in his own estimation and according to his own confession and the confession of his. followers is here especially to champion the farmers-objecting to a duty of 12i per cent on a mower, of 12i per cent on a binder or a reaper, as robbing the farmer, and at the same time taking out of the pockets of the farmers over 21 per cent profit for his own company. These gentlemen may be able to get away with that sort of thing out west, but I want to assure them that so far as Eastern Canada is concerned-and I am perfectly certain I can say so far as the province of Ontario is concerned-he cannot pull the wool over the eyes of the farmers. They may be able to justify themselves in finding fault with the Government for imposing a duty which would mean -say, $31 on a binder, while at the same time they take out of the pocket of the farmer over $52 and put it in their own treasury in the way of profits for themselves; they may be able to justify themselves out west by objecting to the Government taking an average of $14.64 in the way of a tariff on farm implements while they at the same time take $21.06 profits for themselves on farm implements. They get over that very conveniently, or think they do, by telling the farmers in the West "Oh, you are partners in this concern and we are giving you a part of the profits- you will get that in the shape of dividends." Well, there is some of it that I believe they do not get in the shape of dividends. In one year their profits on implements, according to the sworn statement of Mr. Rice Jones, amounted to $272,215. Yet they believe in free implements or say they do. In one year their profits on lumber- another thing that they want free of duty -were $68,383. Then we have the statement from the hon. member for Marquette-
Mr. REID (Mackenzie); Will the hon. member give us the number of thousand feet of lumber that profit was made on?

I do not know whether I can give it or not. It may be in the evidence of Mr. Rice Jones but I do not think that matters at all. My hon. friend and his, leader have stood up in this House time and again and spoken of the aggregate profits made by the Monarch Knitting Company, the Dominion Textiles, and so on, and they do not divide those profits by anything; but when it comes to themselves, when their own foot is pinched, they say "Oh you divide the profit that was made by the number of bushels of grain, or by the number of feet of lumber we handled"; they do not for one moment, allow any other company in the Dominion to do the same sort of thing. The hon. member for Marquette, in answer to the member for Annapolis (Mr. Davidson), said he thought the duty on apples should be removed, and that, apples should be free. But he and his company could soak the farmer to the extent of some fourteen or fifteen thousand dollars profits in one year in handling a few barrels of apples, and they could shove that into their treasury. In two years, 1916 and 1917, their profits amounted to $1,699,689, according to the sworn evidence of Mr. Rice Jones, and those were the two years when the war was on-war years, war profits, war profiteers! We have heard the word "profiteers" quite frequently from hon. gentlemen opposite. Now I want to show, Sir, that if hon. gentlemen opposite are justified i nreferring to any company in this country which makes a profit of 38 or 40 per cent as war profiteers, the company of which the hon. member for Marquette is president comes under that censure because according to Rice Jones' sworn evidence it made in one year a profit of 62.2 per cent, and in another year a profit of 44.9 per cent; and in the case of its New York subsidiary company-according again to the statement of Rice Jones, the $13,000 manager, corroborated on the floor of this House by the $15,000 president, the member for Marquette-on $100,000 invested in the New York Export Company it made in one year a profit of $530,000 or 530 per cent.
Hear, hear.

Of course, I understand my hon. friend from Mackenzie is interested in that company and it gives him joy to think of the amount of money it has been able to make. Where did the hon. gentleman and his friends get this money? Every dollar that the Grain
Growers Grain Company has made in the way of profits has come out of the farmer in one way or another. It has come in the way of profits on grain that they bought from the farmer, or it has come in the way of profits on goods of one kind oi another that they sold back to the farmer, and the hon. gentleman says "hear, hear", Certainly, that pleases him. It is not going to please the farmers of the West as soon as they understand-and they will understand before very long-just how far these hon. gent'emen go. It is ail right enough for a certain hon. gentleman drawing $15,000 salary, others drawing $13,000, others drawing $11,000, and others looking forward to drawing that much or more, to say "Hear, hear." This is the sort of thing that appeals to them. Mr. Speaker, I want to say right here that the Dominion Textile Company, the Canners Company, and some of these other companies which have been referred to by hon. gentlemen opposite, are not living up to their opportunities if they do not raise the salary bid and get the hon. member for Marquette to be president of one of these companies, the hon. member for Mackenzie to be manager and the hon. member for Red Deer to be secretary. Yes, Mr. Speaker, I venture to say the moment it is mentioned in the press of this country that the hon. member for Marquette has become the president of any one of these companies its stock will go up sky high.
They are money makers all right.

A man who exhibits to the degree that the hon. member for Marquette does the facility for feasting at the farmer's table and filching his spoons is a man who ought to make any company rich if he only had the management of it. Where did they get some of this money? In five years, according to the sworn testimony of Rice Jones, they took 367,000 bushels of grain out of the farmers in overages. They did that to protect themselves from a shortage of 3,800 bushels! That is what you might call playing "safety first." That was worth,, according to the same authority, $418,000. The overage did not belong to the company, it did not belong to the president of the company or to those who were fortunate enough to have a block of stock in it, but it belonged to the farmers of Western Canada, and they took that money out of the pockets of those farmers and put it in their own treasury. Then they had an-

other chance to make money on the side in regard to screenings. Taking the six years, including the last years of the war, the average price of screenings was $8.84, but in 1918, when the hon. member for Marquette, the president of the Grain Growers' Grain Company, was Minister of Agriculture, he bought screenings from those various companies, and the hon. member for Maple Creek (Mr. Maharg) knows very well that the president of the Grain Growers' Grain Company got quite a lot from him at $35 a ton.
What year was that?
1918, I think.
They did not get any screenings from the company that I represent.

Yes, they got 1,330 tons and paid $46,560 for them. That is once where the president of the Grain Growers' Comany put one over the Minister of Agriculture. I might also call attention to how anxious this special pleader for the farmers was to assist them. He commandeered the butter which was being made-not which had been made-at 46i cents a pound at the very time when there were over 27,000,000 pounds of butter in cold storage in various parts of the country; and yet he posed as the great friend of the farmers.
Now, for political purposes, there has been so much misrepresentation on the other side of the House as to the attitude and policy of the right hon. Prime Minister on the tariff and he has been so frequently portrayed as a high protectionist, that I want to place on Hansard the words which the right hon. gentleman delivered in this House on May 25 last year. At page 2708 of Hansard for 1920 it will be found that in referring to the tariff he said:
This is the tariff, and not higher, but lower than that adopted by hon. gentlemen opposite when they were in office under circumstances of far less urgent need. It is admitted to be a tariff which is lower than that which hon. gentlemen opposite unanimously supported all through thqse fifteen years. It is a tariff not designed to benefit the rich in this country; it is designed, so far as our own information goes- and it cannot be complete without investigation -only to give such measure of assistance as to retain within this country its industrial strength, and which does not alienate from this country a measure of the industrial strength that we have. We never can have a high tariff in Canada. We connat have a high tariff in Canada for the most obvious reasons. In the first place, a high tariff is unsound in principle in that it tends to eliminate one of the factors of com-

petition, namely, foreign goods. Foreign goods should be allowed to enter into competition under fair conditions in this or in any other country. But the conditions under free trade or without protection are sucn that the foreign competitor has every advantage.
The principle enunciated in those remarks has been endorsed at various times and in almost similar words by the late Sir John A. Macdonald, the late Sir Wilfrid Laurier, the hon. member for King's, N.S. (Sir Robert Borden), the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) and, I may say, by all other prominent public men in this country who lay any claim to statemanship. As against the opinions of these men we have a few free trade theorists who denounce protection as a vice. That is done repeatedly by the hon. member for Red Deer, by the hon. member for Marquette, by the hon. member for Brome and by others when they want to bolster up their free trade doctrines.
What does the hon. gentleman say I have been doing?

I will tell the hon.
gentleman what he has been doing, and I do not think that it will sit very well on his stomach. These hon. gentlemen say, "If protection is a good thing, why not go the limit and make your wall so high as to exclude all goods?"

Very wise language it may be, but it seems to me to be very inconsistent with the vociferous expressions of free trade opinion which my hon. friend voices on occasions. He denounces protection as a curse, but he says it would be wise to retain the curse for a while-to get rid of it gradually. One would naturally suppose that if protection was a curse and free trade a benefit, the sooner you got rid of the curse and acquired the benefit, the better it would be for the country. But my hon. friend says that is not the way to do it. "Protection is a curse, but don't you fellows think we are going to do away with it all at once; we will hang on to it for a little while." He says: Protection is a violation of sound economics, of sane reasoning and of elemental, common sense. But for practical political purposes, both he and his party are perfectly willing to follow a line of policy which is not sound economics, which is not sane and which is not good common sense. To argue that the proper thing to do is to eliminate a vicious thing by degrees, is to admit that a measure of political vice is preferable to complete virtue. I am reminded of the lines:
Vice is a monster of so frightful mien,
As, to be hated, needs but to be seen;
Vet seen too oft, familiar with her face,
We first endure, then pity, then embrace.
I am afraid the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark) is actually degenerating; he is becoming rather familiar with this vice; he wants to coddle it along now for practical political purposes. He is making his appeal now to the manufacturers of the country. I venture to guess that in certain parts of the West he would not use that kind of language at all; but in

certain parts of Ontario and in certain parts of Quebec and the Maritime Provinces, it is good practical politics to play the other side of the game, to play, in fact, a double game. Yet the hon. member for Red Deer said on that occasion:
I do not know exactly where the official Opposition stands in regard to this question of trade, but we of the progressive party are not in any douibt as to where we stand.
For practical political purposes, I can tell them just where they stand. They stand exactly where the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) stands- all things to all men, ready to play the game of free trade when it suits their constituencies to do so, and ready to pander to the manufacturers where they think they can get a few votes by that means. Not one of them has yet dared to try out those wings in testing this House as regards the theories which they profess. They seem to be afraid of one another. They denounce protection in that degree; but they seem to be afraid to put the matter to the test for fear that some persons will not see the thing just as they do. So they carry on this policy of deception.

they will wind up by voting for anything which is moved against this Government. They think that they can pull the wool over the eyes of the people in this country and that the people will swallow that sort of thing. I can tell my hon. friends that the people will not do that. The hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's has made a statement regarding the Liberal party not favouring free trade, and he has also made the same statement in regard to the party led by the hon. member for Marquete. Last session, in this House, the hon. member for North Perth (Mr. Morphy) put this question to the hon. member for Marquette:
Mr. Morphy: The hon. gentleman has been quoting authorities in favour of free trade, but is he himself In favour of free trade for Canada?
Mr. Crerar: I will say this, that the fiscal policy for Great Britain, in my judgment, would be a very admirable one for Canada.
We all know what the fiscal, policy of Great Britain is. It is a free trade policy, and it seems to me that the hon. member for Marquette, the leader of the Progressive party, in making that statement, announced himself as a free trader. I should like to quote one other observation which he made on the same occasion and this is to be found in Hansard of May 31, 1920, page 2908:
I have never been able to see the sense of creating-, for instance, a cotton industry in Can-a^a

which I shall refer to in a moment-and which is entirely an artificial industry in this country.
I quote that because it is in line with statements made by the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's this
10 p.m. afternoon. If those words mean anything at all, they mean that the hon. member for Marquette, if he had his way, wuold wipe out every cotton industry in the Dominion of Canada. If those words do not mean that, 1 do not understand the English language. I do not know any other construction that you can put on his words.
Free trade, as they have it in England, will be, the hon. member for Marquette says, a fine thing for this country. I represent a rural constituency, and I want to discuss the question of free trade for a few minutes as to how that policy as advocated
by the hon. member for Marquette would affect the farmers of this country if it were put into effect. I want to call the attention of the House to a statement made by Cob-den in 1844. I trust the hon. member for Red Deer will forgive me if I undertake to quote some of those illustrious gentlemen whom he has quoted so frequently in this House. I do not suppose he wants a monopoly of the quoting of their names and utterances. At all events I will run the risk of quoting them.
I forgive the hon. gentleman freely.

My hon. friend's generosity is simply marvellous. I thank him very much. In 1844, Cobden said:
Free trade in corn is the very way to increase the .production at home and stimulate the production of the poorest soils by compelling the application of more capital and labour to them. We do not contemplate deriving one bushel less corn from the soil of this country.
Gobden proved to be a mighty poor prophet. Thompson was more honest than his companion, when, in his "Free Trade Catechism" he wrote:
It may be information to the home agriculturists to state that "there would be no physical impossibility in living without them altogether."
Some hon. members in this House seem to think the same now. In 1853, there were
4.200.000	acres in wheat in the United Kingdom. In 1910, there were 1,856,000 acres. In 1870, Great Britain and Ireland produced
13.500.000	quarters of wheat; in 1910, only 7,000,000 quarters. Cobden's prophecy was evidently a very poor one. Taking'the 105 registration districts which, in 1911, contained no portion of an urban district, I find that in the fifty years between 1801 and 1851, the agricultural population of the United Kingdom increased, and that in the next fifty years it decreased. There was a steady increase in each de-cennium under protection and a steady decline in each decennium under free trade. I would like the hon. member for Marquette, particularly to note that, because he has gone on record several times as saying that the decline in rural population in Canada is due to our policy of protection. Each census of the United Kingdom for the past forty years shows a decrease in the acreage of arable land and a corresponding increase in the acreage of grass land. This retrograde movement in agriculture has caused British statesmen considerable alarm, and has led to a very careful and special investigation. The

"I believe we are very near getting to a point where our agricultural industry will be entirely secondary and our agricultural population reduced to a most dangerously low proportion. Another quotation from Sir A. Boscawen:
"Free trade has made us dangerously dependent on foreign countries for our food supplies and has depopulated our country districts and massed the people more and more into our *big towns."
These are expressions of opinion which cannot lightly be passed over. In this connection may I quQte from the speech made by the hon. member for Marquette last year. He said:
"My hon. friend the Prime Minister (Mr. Meighen) also speaks of the decline of agriculture in Great Britain, and he attributes that decline to the fact that Great Britain is a free trade country. If my hon. friend seeks a reason for the decline of agriculture in Great Britain, if there has been a decline, he will find it in the land policy of the Old Country, and not in the free trade policy that obtains there. When my hon. friends says that agriculture is declining in Great Britain because a free trade policy has been in operation there for the past 70 years, he is unquestionably very wide of the mark."
I have given you not mere haphazard opinions, but the opinions of members of the British Government up to as late as December of last year, and their opinions do not agree at all with the opinions of the hon. member for Marquette.
I want to place a few more statements on Hansard in regard to this question of free trade, and I do so because the hon. member for Red Deer has, for the last ten or twelve years, ever since he became a member for this House, been voicing his free trade opinions and quoting British authorities and all that sort of thing, in an endeavour to influence public opinion in this country. He has a few disciples who, in somewhat weaker voice, echo his remarks; and for that reason, because I believe his arguments are fallacious, and because he has been putting before the country a lot of free trade folly, I want to call the attention of hon. members to a few further facts in regard to the way in which this policy has worked out in Great Britain, and the effect it has had upon agriculture in that country.
In 1860 Great Britain had 4,019,735 acres sown to wheat which produced 13,135,124 quarters, and her imports of wheat and flour were 7,364,439 quarters. In 1914 Great Britain had only 1,904,932 acres in wheat, which produced 7,804,041 quarters, and their imports were 27,509,031 quarters.
In 1870 Great Britain had 24,092,075 acres of arable land and 22,085,295 acres in pasture. By 1914 the arable land was reduced to 19,414,166 acres and the pasture land increased to 27,349,650 acres. Between 1871 and 1911 the number of farmers and farm employees had decreased by 684,256.
In 1870 the average prices were: Wheat 46/ lid, per quarter, barley 34/ 7d, oats 22/ 10d., beef 41d. per pound, mutton 51d. per pound, wool 16id. per pound.
In 1914 the average prices were: Wheat 34/ lid., barley 27/ 2d., oats 20/ lid., beef 3!d., mutton 4d., wool 1/ 2d. (12!d.) per pound.
The above figures show just how agriculture has declined in Great Britain, and what its position was in August, 1914. Why was it that British agriculture had been declining and its output dwindling, and cheap food from overseas playing an increasingly dominant part in supplying the needs of the people, while the exact opposite was taking place in Germany, a country that possessed, on the whole, a poorer soil and a less favourable climate? I wish to quote, in this connection, the words of Mr. T. H. Middleton, C.B., Assistant Secretary of the Board of Agriculture of Great Britain. He says:
"It Is not possible to resist the conclusion that it was the economic policy adopted by his country that prevented the German from following the methods of the British Farmer. The agricultural policy adopted by Germany was indeed extraordinarily successful in restoring confidence and emboldening farmers to resort to intensive cultivation. The main value of the tariff policy to German agriculture was the sense of security which it created in the farmer. It was the conviction that he was essential to the community; and it may be added that it was the knowledge that hLs grain was not wanted, and that his fellow countrymen did not depend upon his exertions that led the British Farmer at the same period to cut down expenses and reduce or at least fail to increase the productivity of his land."
Now, that is the situation. May I just refer to one industry other than farming? If free trade is a policy which cannot be assailed on the ground of unsoundness, then, Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that inasmuch as Great Britain had, at the time of adopting free trade, a lead in manufactur-

ing over any other country in the world- I do not think that any one will question that fact-and if protection was a bad policy, and one that would operate to the detriment of the country that adopted it, then Great Britain should be in a vastly better position to-day, in regard to manufacturers, than she is. Inasmuch as Great Britain, at the time she adopted free trade, had a start over every other country in manufacturing, surely, if her policy was right, she not only should have maintained her lead, but should have increased it.
Let me.refer to one industry. In 1880 Great Britain produced 8,000,000 tons, Germany about 3,000,000 tons, and the United States about 4,000,000 tons, of pig iron. By 1888, the United States had forced Great Britain into second place, and by 1902, Germany had forced Great Britain to take third place. True, free traders may say that between 1880 and 1910, British production of pdg iron had steadily increased from 8,000,000 to 10,000,000 tons under free trade. In answer to that I say that in the United States, in the same length of time, the production increased from 4,000,000 to 27,000,000 and in Germany from 3,000,000 to 14,500,000 tons- in Germany and the United States, under a *policy of protection, and in Great Britain, under free trade. Mr. Speaker, we cannot get away from this fact:	Great Britain,
under her free trade policy, has been forced by her own fiscal system to pass remedial legislation for the benefit of the farmers of the country. Under free trade agriculture has been ruined in Great Britain to such an extent that to-day that country is Obliged to pass legislation guaranteeing the prices of certain commodities to the farmers. She has to put her hand into the public treasury in order to subsidize the farmers in the growing of certain products, and that is the policy which the hon. member for Marquette says appeals to him as one that would be in the interests of the farmers of this country.
Now, Sir, the hon. member for Marquette has referred at various times to the province of Ontario, which he has misrepresented, and for that reason I wailt to place on Hansard some facts in regard to that province. I take my facts from a source which the hon. member for Marquette will hardly question on the ground of reliability. I take them from a report issued by the Drury Government under the imprimatur of the Hon. Mr. Manning Doherty, the Minister of Agriculture in that Govern-

ment. Between 1898 and 1908 the number of farms in Ontario increased from 177,000 to 183,000, and the mortgages on farms and farm stock decreased by over $65,000,000; while in the same time the number of farms in Michigan increased from 175,000 to 178,000, and the mortgages on farms and livestock increased by $79,898,000. The state of Michigan had no tariff barriers to keep the produce of its farmers out of the big centres of population on the other side of the line. Now, comparing 1919 with 1909, Ontario shows an increase of 441,758 acres in assessed land. It shows 640,670 acres increase in cleared land, and increase of 549,803 acres in slash land-that is land partly cleared- a decrease of 267,025 acres in swamp or waste land-showing that that land had been re-claimed. Every county in the province of Ontario, except three, shows an increase in the acreage cleared in the last ten years, and there has been a decrease in the number of chattel mortgages against farmers from 6,816 in 1899 to 3,457 in 1919, the total decrease amounting to $290,583. The acreage under all field crops increased by 812,091 acres in the ten years, and the value of products by $238,077,019. Ontario in the ten years shows the following increases: In the value of land $167,978,000; buildings $128,958,000; implements $59,519,000; livestock $511,315,000; total $867,772,327. Remember these are increases in the last ten years, a showing unequalled, I venture to say, by any state in the American Union. In addition to the value of livestock, let me add that the horses, cattle, sheep, swine and poultry sold or slaughtered in 1919 had a value of more than 851 million dollars in excess of that of 1909.
Now, Sir, I want to invite your attention just for a few minutes to some figures, which I will place on Hansard, along this line in regard to the United States-figures which are to me very significant, and I will promise the House not to be very much longer. I want to say that there was an increase in the number of farms in the United States between 1900 and 1910 of 624,130. Between 1910 and 1920 there was an increase of only 88,496 farms. Mr. Speaker, will you please give your attention to this fact, that out of forty-eight states in the American Union, twelve showed a decrease and thirty-six showed an increase in the number of farms in 1910 as compared with 1900. Now note this fact: In the census of 1920, twenty-five of the forty-eight states show a decrease in the number of farms, and twenty-three an increase in

the number of farms, as compared with ten years ago. It will perhaps he of special interest to the people of Ontario to know that the states of New York, Pennsylvania, Ohio, and Michigan had 17,051 fewer farms in 1910	than in	1900,	and thatthese same states show a further decrease	of 65,235	farms in	1920
as compared with 1910-that is a decrease of 82,286 farms in those four states in the last twenty years, and they are right close to the big centres of population. The people of Quebec and the Maritime Provinces may be interested in the fact that the states of Maine, New Hamp. shire, Massachusetts and Vermont had 2,747 fewer farms in 1910 than in 1900, and a further reduction of 17,741 between 1910 and 1920. Add to the eight states I have already given you, the states of Con: necticut, Delaware, Maryland, New Jersey, Rhode Island, Illinois, Indiana and Iowa, which show a reduction of 26,711 farms between 1900 and 1910, and a further reduction of 50,710 between 1910 and 1920, and you have the startling fact that in the sixteen states I have named, and which are close to Canada, there are 192,110 fewer farms to-day than twenty years ago, and that the big part of the reduction has taken place in the last ten years. I do not think we need wonder, Mr. Speaker, that the United States Congress has seen fit to introduce an emergency tariff Bill for the protection of the farmers of that country. But, Sir, I want to call your attention to another fact. Not only do twenty-five of the fourty-eight states show a reduction in the number of farms, but they show a decrease in the farm acreage and in the improved acreage amounting to millions of acres in the aggregate. The farm mortgage indebtedness represents a higher percentage of the actual land values than it did ten years a^o. I want my hon. friend from Marquette, when he is trying to make an argument to influence the farmers of Ontario and the people of this country by trying to make them believe that they have abandoned farms in Ontario, to consider the figures that I have given and compare the states just across the line with the province of Ontario. I may say, Mr. Speaker, and I give it to you as my firm conviction-although I have not gone into the figures-that I believe, in so far as farm acreage and improved farm acreage are concerned, the province of Quebec will make a better showing in the last ten years than did the province of Ontario in that regard.
I want to call your attention to a very significant fact. When I found that twenty-five of the states on the other side of the line showed a decrease in the number of farms I naturally began to look around to see how matters stood with the states just across the line from Ontario. I followed that up and I found that with possibly two exceptions, speaking from memory, all of the twenty-five states which show a decrease in the number of farms in the last ten years are northern states, are states which have a climate similar to the climate that we have in Ontario, Quebec and the Maritime Provinces. The states which show an increase in the number of farms and in the improved farm acreage are the states of California, Oregon, Washington, Texas, North Carolina, Virginia, and so on-those states which have a decided advantage over the northern states in that they do not have a winter to contend with. It is impossible for the United States Government to draw a line between those states which have a climate similar to ours, and those states in the south which have a mild climate, and place a duty on the products of those southern states as a means of protecting the producers of the same articles in the northern states. They cannot very well do that. But can we get over the significance of the fact that the states which show an increase in the number of farms and in the improved acreage are those which do not have a winter to contend with, and that those states which are in the north and which have a winter -states like Ohio and Illinois, and no person will question the fertility of the soil of those states-show a decrease in the number of farms and in the improved acreage.
What is the conclusion? That the farmers of those states cannot compete on even terms with the farmers who are more advantageously situated in the southern part of the country. Now, while the United States cannot put up a barrier against the farmers of the South, we are in the position of being able to protect our farmers from the unfair competition of their rivals in the southern and southwestern states where they have the advantage of a mild climate. Our farmers can produce only one crop a year; there they produce two or three crops annually. Our farmers and those of New York, Pennsylvania and Michigan are in the same position in that they have to spend thousands of dollars on barns and stables to protect their stock

during the winter months, while the stock of the southern farmers is roaming outside all the winter. That is a capital investment which our farmers must get a return on. Furthermore, they have to spend more money in this northern country in houses and clothing to protect themselves against the winter weather than have their competitors in the states of Texas, Oklahoma and Oregon; in' fact, in those states the mild winter renders unnecessary this extra expense.
And yet my hon. friends opposite announce as their policy that if they have the opportunity they will oblige our farmers to compete on even terms not only with the farmers of the southern and southwestern states, but with tliose of the Argentine, Brazil and other countries where they have the double advantage of cheap labour and a mild climate. I cannot conceive of anything more unfair and unreasonable than such a policy. The hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) gave us to understand this afternoon that the Liberal party is not a free trade party. Other hon. gentlemen in order to gain votes from those interested-in the industries of this country say that they will not at one fell swoop do away with tariff protection for manufactured goods because that would cause too much economic disturbance; while they believe in a policy of free trade they assure manufacturers that they will introduce it gradually. Mr. Speaker, have the manufacturing concerns in the Dominion as much money invested in their factories as the farmers have invested in their land, buildings, stock and implements? If free trade is such a good thing, why is it proposed only to bring it in gradually in regard to manufactured articles, but at one fell swoop so far as farm products are concerned? I maintain that their attitude is most inconsistent and most unfair.
In this period of reconstruction, Mr. Speaker, the man who is first going to feel the decline in prices is the farmer. That is quite evident to-day. I take up the paper and find that butter is offered in the city of Montreal at 25 cents and a fraction a pound.' And right here I want to say, as one representing an agricultural constituency, that I am not at all satisfied with the Budget in so far as butter and oleomargarine are concerned. It is absolutely* illogical and unfair to allow oleomargarine to be imported free of duty while four cents a pound is imposed on butter. If you say, "We have a duty of 4

cents a pound on butter for the protection of the farmers who produce that article," then how in the name of common sense can you say that it is proper to allow oleomargarine to come in without any duty at all? It certainly takes the place of butter. Last year it displaced butter in this country to the extent of some seven million pounds imported from the United States.
Hon. gentlemen opposite talk sometimes about the United States being the great natural market for the surplus farm products of Canada. That is absolute nonsense, and if instead of preparing theses on free trade hon. gentlemen opposite would take the trouble to acquaint themselves with certain facts in regard to farm production in the United States and in Canada they would not make such a ridiculous statement. The natural market for our surplus farm products is not where they have a greater surplue of those farm products than we have, but in those countries where they lack those products. On that basis I want to say that the United States is not the natural market for surplus Canadian farm products. Last year we had a surplus of 17,470,000 pounds of butter, but the United States exported over
34,400,000	pounds of butter and oleomargarine, and they supplied us with 7,352,000 pounds of that butter and oleomargarine, for which we paid them $2,275,547. When I see the farmers of the Dominion hunting all over God's creation to find a market for their surplus butter and finally selling it to some thirty-five different countries, practically greasing the whole globe in order to dispose of that surplus, and at the same time the United States is allowed to export to this country butter and eleomargarine to the extent of millions of pounds, and forcing our own butter off the home market, I state frankly that if I were handling the tariff I would say, " The duty on butter is not as high as it ought to be," and I would increase that duty. The same thing applies in regard to eggs. The United States'had a surplus of 25,183,000 dozen and sold us 7,000,000 dozen, for which we paid then! $3,333,658, although we had 5,800,000 dozen of our own eggs to dispose of. My conclusion is that when we were forced to hunt for markets all over the globe to sell those eggs, and at the same time imported 7,000,000 dozen from the United tates, our duty on eggs is not as high as it ought to be for the protection of our farmers. Canada's surplus milk last year amounted to $2,500,000 worth, as against the United States

surplus of $59,204,000. Does that look as if the United States provides a market for our milk? They ship milk in here in the form of cheese and condensed milk. Canada's surplus meat last year amounted to
260,100,000	pounds, and we had to look all over the world to find a market for it; at the same time the United States had a surplus of 1,663,700,000 pounds. Yet notwithstanding our own surplus of meat and dairy products for which we had to find a market in a great many countries, the United tates sold us last year over $10,000,000 worth of meat and over $7,790,000 worth of dairy products. I argue from that condition of affairs that the duty at present is not as high as it should he. in the interests of the Canadian farmer who is producing these articles. The Canadian farmer is entitled, just as the Canadian manufacturer is entitled, to the first chance to sell his products in thq home market. To tell him that he mustx compete on even terms with the surplus products of the world is to disregard the climatic conditions under which he operates and to treat him most unfairly. To put into effect the policy advocated by the Liberal party in this House, and by the Progressive party as well-for the two policies are the same in regard to making natural products free-to put that into effect will prevent the Canadian farmers from getting the highest prices for anything that they have to sell. Just as soon as prices in Canada become high enough to attract these products from other countries, if our doors are open they will come in and take advantage of those prices, while the countries from which they come will keep up their tariff walls against us. If Australia has surplus eggs to sell and we admit them into Canada free of duty while Australia charges a duty of 12 cents a dozen on eggs going into their country, is that fair? Is that reasonable? Is that honest treatment for the farmers of this country? In my estimation, it is not. I know that the leader of the Opposition is the father of this idea. I know that he it was who some years ago, after making a careful study of the matter, after noticing that the farmers were getting such prices as 16 cents a pound for butter, 7 cents a pound for cheese, 6i cents a dozen for eggs, 18 cents a bag for potatoes, and so on-he it was who proposed the policy of opening the doors of Canada and letting the surplus products of the world come into this country free so as to bring the prices down still lower. He said at that time that the country was on the verge
of a revolution because of the high prices the farmers were getting for their products. He advocates the same thing today, namely, that our doors should be open to allow the surplus products of the world to come in here while other countries retain their tariff walls against us. Mr. Speaker, I protest against that as most unfair to the farmers of this country. The farmers do not ask any favour, but they do ask for a fair deal, and a fair deal in my judgment they are not getting at the present time. After all, the great producers, the great manufacturers of this country are the farmers, and they more than any other class of the community deserve to be protected in their own home market. They more than any other class have built up that home market and they should be given the first place in the matter of selling their products in their own home market.
Mr. Speaker, in closing, permit me to express my appreciation of the courtesy and attention with which hon. members of the House have listened to a speech which has been somewhat more lengthy than I anticipated' at the start.
Mr. P. R. Du TREMBLAY (Laurier-Outremont) : Mr. Speaker, at this late hour I shall not undertake to make any extended remarks on the Budget. The hon. member who has just resumed his seat (Mr. Edwards) told us that he favoured the establishment of a permanent commission to revise the tariff. A couple of years ago I made that suggestion to the Government, but I must say that it seemed to fall on deaf ears. At that time I thought it would be a good thing, but I have changed my mind; I believe that the Government should take the responsibility in respect to tariff changes. But it does not appear to be the intention of the Government to make any change in the tariff, and that is why I think the reason given by the Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) in his able speech of yesterday evening is hardly the real reason for the Government not making any change in the tariff. I really think the Government are afraid to touch this question, in view of the fact that an election is coming very soon, or within a year or so. The Government would like to have the support as far as possible of the big interests, and, on the other hand, they want to make the consumers of the country believe that they are doing something in the way of lightening their burdens.
I do not think that the suggestion of the Finance Minister that the action of the

United States in connection with tariff changes would affect this country is a very sound one. At the time when the speech from the Throne was delivered the Fordney Bill was before the country and it was known what that Bill contemplated and what its effect would be upon Canada. So that the reasons given by the minister and by the hon. member for Frontenac, are, in my opinion, only apparent reasons; they do not meet the real issue. During two or three sessions tariff changes have repeatedly been promised. Hon. gentlemen all remember that two or three years ago we were to have this revision of the tariff. Last year it was arranged that a special commission should travel about the country and obtain information from the different interests upon which tariff revision could be based. The Minister of Finance presided at those meetings in such a way as to merit the appreciation of the people; he had a pleasant trip throughout the country, but I am sorry that he did not come to the conclusion to give the country the benefit of that work and those conferences in the form of tariff changes at this session.
I wish to congratulate the minister for the moderate changes he has made in the tariff as outlined in his Budget speech. I really think the minister has shown a laudable desire to assist the business interests of this country. I know that he likes to hear the other man's views; he likes to learn, and he is always very desirous of doing the best he can for this country. But I know, at the same time, that he has the thankless task of collecting as much money as possible so that his colleagues in the different departments may spend it as quickly as it comes in. I do not intend to hold him responsible for all the sins of Israel, for all that this Government has done. He is rather a young man in politics and before he came into the Government almost all the wrong was done. There is not much change in the present legislation. It is moderate. I must say that I approve dropping the business tax and I will say that I do not disapprove the other changes of minor importance as regards liquor and so on. It is, however, because the changes are rather too moderate that I would complain. As I said a minute ago, the people at large had been expecting a general change in the tariff. There is in this country the feeling that the Government represents the big interests, the rich people; that it does not sufficiently protect the poor consumer, and the people thought that at this session something would be done towards reducing

the high cost of living. That has not been done. Although there is not much change, the wrong that I spoke of a minute ago still remains; the heavy debt contracted by this Government, the unfair, unjust taxation imposed on the people during the last five or six years still exists, and if you go to any place in the country to-day, you will find a feeling of unrest.
It is, perhaps, no secret to the Government that it will have difficulty in finding, amongst business men, many who approve its conduct in administering the affairs of the country, especially since the end of the war. Nearly all business men in Canada are against the Government, and when the elections take place, the Government will fare badly.
What is the condition of affairs to-day? I was speaking of the business men especially, because members of the Government often speak about the business interests of this country. The general feeling throughout the country is really one of discouragement, because the people feel that the Government is watching them in the enterprises that they undertake. The people have to pay heavy taxes in customs and excise, on cheques, on notes, and on many necessities of life, and then if they dare to make a litle money by their efforts or energy, they feel that the Government is watching them, ready to take them by the throat and take away part of their little profit by means of the income tax. This is a time when individual enterprise and energy should be given encouragement.
The Minister of Finance told us that, in round figures, the public debt of Canada was about $2,350,000,000. I do not know if this huge sum of money comprises the obligations of the different railways such as the Grand Trunk and the Canadian National railways. A debt of $2,350,000,000 means a debt of $300 per capita for every man, woman and child in Canada. If you take a father with his wife and three children, that means that he owes $1,500 for himself and his family. If you take into consideration what the people owe for their provincial debt, for their muni-
11 p.m. cipal debt, you will come to the same conclusion as thoughtful business men who realize that the country is not on the road to prosperity. The proposed expenditure for next year, according to the minister, will be about $435,000,000. We must add to this obligations that we have to meet for the railways, obligations which I understand are in the neighbourhood of $137,000,000. That makes a total

of $582,000,000. As the revenue supposed to be available is $372,000,000, you have really a deficit of $210,000,000 to meet this year. My hon. friends opposite may say to me: "Well, it is only for this year that we have to meet these extra obligations for the railways." But according to men who know, and according to the way the situation appears to-day, we shall have a recurring deficit of between one hundred and two hundred million dollars on account of railways.
The Minister of Finance, in his very learned and capable speech, referred to the golden times of the Liberal party, which assumed office in 1896, and whose long and prosperous administration we recall with pleasure. Let us compare the condition then with the position in which the country is now. At that time the public debt of Canada was about $340,000,000 or about $42 per capita. That amount represented all the money that had been spent to build up the country, by way of subsidies, to assist the construction of railways, and expenditures on post offices, wharves and other public necessities. What do we spend this year? $582,000,000, or $73 per capita. That is to say, we are spending this year for the administration of this country two-thirds more than our entire debt in 1911. It is no use of hiding our heads in the sand like the ostrich; we may as well look the facts in the face. We are to-day spending nearly twice as much as the entire national debt in 1911. That is why the people, and very properly so, do not think our financial position is very good, and why they are calling for a halt on the Government spending millions as if they were thousands. I am pleased to see the Prime Minister in his seat, also the Minister of Finance. I want to tell them that that is the message of the people of the country and of the business men of Montreal.
The Government may ask me what I suggest as a remedy, and in reply to my suggestion they may say, as they usually do: Oh, but our present condition is the result of the war; we have been through a war, and we have had to spend millions on this and that. I would very humbly suggest that if the Government are in earnest, if they are strong enough, if they are sufficiently independent of strong "pull," if they really want to do something for the good of this country, if they really want to put aside patronage and adopt some other method of administration, there is still hope for Canada-I will not say, of getting
on a sound business basis-but of being able to make a fresh start and to gradually pay off her debt.
I would suggest that the Government should give up now and completely their policy in regard to the railroads. Give the railroads away. A proposition was made some days ago by the Canadian Pacific. I do not say that that proposition was the best that could be made, but if it is necessary, pay the Canadian Pacific to take these roads over, because the Government will never make money out of them. They will always be a burden. Why? Because you have too much expenditure on management for instance. It is nothing new that I say. Any capable railway official will tell you that parallel railways are a big expense to a country and must be operated at a loss. Take, for instance, a district that I know well, between Ottawa and Montreal. You have every day of the week about ten trains coming over the Canadian Pacific from Montreal to Ottawa, about seven over the Grand Trunk, and four over the Canadian Northern. Why is this? From information that has been given to me I believe that ten trains would cover this whole district that is to-day served by over twenty. It is this duplication that adds to the expense, and we know that in winter the expense is. especially heavy. So I say it would pay the Government to get rid of these roads, but I do not suppose the Government will do it, and I will tell you frankly why. The Government wants to keep the roads on account of the patronage it can exercise in connection with them. The Government may say that there is no more patronage, but the people of this country know to the contrary. It is no use trying to hide the fact. The people know why the Government want to keep and operate these railways.
I could say the same thing with regard to the Canadian Government Merchant Marine. Why not sell these ships? You will lose probably about $20,000,000 if you sell this year, but it is better to take that loss now than to continue your losses from year to year. The report of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Ballantyne) issued in December last is not very encouraging. I know him well; I know he has good intentions; I know he did his best, and that under the present conditions he could not do much better. It is not his fault; it is the trade conditions in this and other countries. Probably the
